title: The Grand Survey
part: PART ONE: THE SHOP AT THE END OF INK LANE

pages.text:
*The Second Rule of Mapmaking: Start where you stand.*

The crowd in Ink Lane was thick and noisy, a tangle of wool coats and leather boots pressing against the damp cobblestones. A large sheet of parchment was nailed to the town post, fluttering in the cold breeze. Tam pushed through, her patched brown coat brushing against a merchant’s sleeve, and began to read.

She read it three times. The first time, her eyes slid over the words because they were too big and important. The second time, she sounded out the letters, moving her finger under each word as if it were a row of teeth. The third time, she let the meaning settle. Twenty-one days. The Uncharted Marches. Every apprentice in the kingdom.

A girl in a blue velvet cloak, her hair pinned with pearls, stood directly behind Tam. Tam felt the girl’s eyes on her ink-stained fingers, on her worn shoes, on the blue string in her braid. Tam did not turn around. She just read the word *winner* again, feeling a hard, cold knot tighten in her stomach, the kind that happens when you drop a full jar of pickles.
pages.image: A sturdy 11-year-old girl with a black braid and ink-stained fingers reads a large parchment nailed to a wooden post, while a girl in a blue velvet cloak watches her from behind in a crowded, misty street.

pages.text:
The Marches were the part of the kingdom nobody liked to talk about. They were wild, tangled, and stubborn, a place of thornwood that snagged your clothes, marshes that swallowed your boots, and moors that stretched out until you forgot where the sky started. No honest map had ever covered them. They were the last blank spot on the royal charts, a hole in the world’s face.

The Academy apprentices were already there, standing in a tight circle near the fountain. Their coats were crisp, their boots polished to a mirror shine. They spoke in low, confident voices, pointing at the parchment as if they had already drawn the lines.

Tam stepped back, her shoulders hunching. "It is not for me," she said. Her voice cut through the mist. "I am not even a proper apprentice. I am the ink grinder. I belong in the shop."

She looked at her hands. They were rough, calloused, and permanently stained black. They were the hands of a dock worker, not a mapmaker. The thought settled in her stomach, cold and heavy.
pages.image: A sturdy 11-year-old girl with a patched brown coat stands apart from a group of well-dressed apprentices in crisp coats near a stone fountain, looking down at her ink-stained hands in a misty town square.

pages.text:
Back in the shop, the smell of dried oak-gall hung in the air, sharp and old. The door banged open, bringing in a gust of wind and three figures. Lucan Ravel stepped in first, his fair hair combed neatly back, his green coat buttoned to the neck. A gold compass swung on a chain at his hip, catching the grey light.

Behind him came Bram, a large boy with gentle eyes, and Ines, small and quick, clutching a stack of papers. Lucan’s eyes swept the room, landing on Tam, who was wiping her hands on her apron.

"Ah, the grinder," Lucan said. His voice was smooth, polite, and sharp as a blade. He did not look at her face. He looked at her hands. "I suppose you will be enjoying the holiday? Of course, there is no question of entering. The Survey is for those who have the training."

Bram shifted uncomfortably, looking at his polished boots. Ines stared at the ceiling. Tam said nothing. She just watched Lucan’s compass swing, back and forth, back and forth, like a pendulum counting down to something she was not ready for.
pages.image: A neat 12-year-old boy in a green coat with silver buttons stands in a shop doorway, a gold compass swinging at his hip, while a sturdy 11-year-old girl with ink-stained fingers watches him from the background.

pages.text:
Master Finch did not turn around. She stood at her desk, back to the door, a quill in her trembling hand. She dipped the nib. She paused. She wrote a single line on thick cream paper.

The scratch of the quill was the only sound.

She blew on the ink. A tiny puff of air, useless against the wetness. Then she turned and handed the sheet to Lucan. He took it, surprised. He read.

Under the heading *Apprentice*, in Finch’s sharp, precise hand, were the words: TAMSIN MARROW.

Lucan’s face went through a series of expressions. It moved across his face like a storm front rolling over a small town. He looked at the name. Then at Tam. Then back at the name.

He folded the paper with excessive care. He tucked it into his coat pocket. It sat there, heavy and undeniable, like a stone in a shoe.

"I will deliver this to the Guild clerks," he said. His voice was tight. "At once."
pages.image: A tall, thin old woman with white hair in a bun and round spectacles hands a small piece of paper to a neat 12-year-old boy in a green coat, who is reading it with a surprised expression in a cluttered shop.

pages.text:
The door clicked shut. The silence that followed was heavy, pressing against Tam’s ears. She looked at Finch, the sound of her own pulse loud in her head, like a drum being beaten inside a tin can.

"You can't," Tam whispered. "I am not... they will laugh at me. They will see I am nothing. I started too far behind."

Finch leaned on her hawthorn cane, her eyes kind and steady. "Rule the Second. Begin where you stand. You are standing in my shop. You have ink under your nails and a story in your hands. You will do."

Tam looked down at her own fingers. The black stains were deep in the whorls of her skin. She thought of the docks, the mud, the years of running errands while other children learned to draw. She was afraid. She was very afraid that she was right, and that the blank space in the map was too big for her to fill.
pages.image: A sturdy 11-year-old girl looks down at her ink-stained hands, her face worried, while a tall, thin old woman with a lavender scarf leans on a hawthorn cane beside her in a dimly lit room.
